revisions.agent_reply:
`policy.py` is written and verified. Final run of `./evaluate.sh` completes all 113 training notes on all 6 charts, every hit judged "perfect", with a mean timing error of about -4 ms and a plan time of 0.1 ms per tick.

**Strategy**

- **Events, not notes.** Each tick the visible notes become candidate landings: every single note, plus every pair of notes within 160 ms and no more than 2.6 lanes apart that can be played by one landing with the gripper opened so each fingertip sits in its own lane. Single notes use the closed gripper, so both fingertips land in one lane.
- **Scheduler.** A small dynamic programme over those events picks the sequence that maximises the number of notes played, subject to the hand being able to lift, travel, change opening, and descend between consecutive landings. Ties are broken by total timing deviation, so chord-style pair landings and deliberately early landings are used only when a note would otherwise be lost. A note may land up to 80 ms early or late, and the predecessor is nudged early when that is what it takes to reach the next one.
- **Commitment.** Once a descent has begun the landing is pinned across ticks, so refinements never cause the hand to bounce back up mid-approach. If half of a chord vanishes from the note list after being judged, the commitment and the gripper opening carry over to the surviving hold or slide.
- **Keyframes.** Lift only as high as the available time allows, travel at hover, wait over the lane, then descend vertically. The touch command is scheduled 25 ms after the hit time because the judge registers contact 4 mm above the surface. Long notes are pressed until their end, or released early at 88% of their duration when the next note needs the hand. Slides follow their waypoints with a 40 ms lead.
- **Calibrated limits.** Experiments with fake extra taps showed the fingertip does not clear the contact band when two touches are closer than about 0.16 s, so the scheduler enforces a 0.19 s minimum between touches. Lateral travel runs at 1.1x the documented comfortable speed, since 1.4x triggered differential-IK limit warnings and cost a short slide.

**What the training charts did not exercise:** chords mixing a tap with a hold or slide, and notes faster than one landing per 0.19 s. The first is handled by the commitment carry-over described above but is untested in simulation. The second is deliberately skipped by the scheduler rather than attempted.

Revision 1 is in place. The training charts were already at 113/113, so this revision targets throughput on denser unseen charts. The final run again completes all 113 notes with every hit judged perfect.

**What changed: a "rocking" landing for two notes close in time**

- **The bottleneck.** My calibration in revision 0 showed that two plain touches by the same fingertips must be about 0.19 s apart, or the second is not "fresh". That caps a one-hand stream at roughly 5 notes per second, and lane changes cost more on top.
- **The new primitive.** For two notes 0.07 to 0.5 s apart and within 2.6 lanes of each other, the hand now lands rolled so only the first fingertip touches, with the other held 10 mm above the screen. At the second note's time the hand rolls flat over 80 ms and the second fingertip lands. Two notes in the same lane are handled by opening the gripper to 40 mm so both tips sit inside the lane. This yields two fresh touches per travel cycle.
- **Scheduling.** Rocking landings are extra candidates in the same dynamic programme, with a small fixed cost so plain landings win whenever they are feasible. The minimum re-tap spacing is enforced from the second touch of a rocked pair.
- **Robustness.** If the first note of a rocked pair is judged and vanishes from the note list before the second lands, the commitment carries over with the roll geometry intact, so the second fingertip still lands on time. Long notes as the second note are released based on when they were actually landed.

**Verification.** I temporarily forced the scheduler to prefer rocking and logged the committed landings. The training charts then used rocked pairs across lanes, in the same lane twice, tap into hold, tap into slide, and the vanishing-first-note case, and every one was judged perfect with 100% hold contact. With the normal cost restored, the charts play exactly as before.

**Limits.** Three notes in one chord still only get two fingertips. Streams faster than about 10 notes per second will still be partially skipped by design rather than attempted and missed.

Revision 2 is in place. The final run completes 113/113 on the training charts, all but one hit judged perfect, mean timing error within 6 ms.

**What changed: "drum" landings while one fingertip stays pressed**

- **The gap this fills.** Revision 1 could only chain two notes per travel cycle, and a hold or slide blocked the whole hand. Real charts constantly put taps during holds, and streams faster than one whole-hand re-touch every 0.19 s.
- **The new mechanism.** The scheduler now tracks an explicit two-fingertip hand state. From any pressed state it may keep one fingertip down and roll the other up, move it (opening the gripper or translating the hand), and roll it down on the next note. The pressed fingertip either stays on its hold or slide, or, if it is only resting on a spent tap, is dragged along. Chains of these landings run without lifting the hand, so taps during holds within two lanes are now playable, and streams can alternate fingertips.
- **Scheduling.** Drum landings are extra options in the same dynamic programme with a small cost, so plain air landings still win whenever they fit. A tie-break prefers the fingertip that has rested longer, and a dragged fingertip is kept on the screen.
- **Keyframes.** The pressed phase is now generated by sampling both fingertip trajectories (press, roll up, move, roll down, drag, follow a slide) and expressing them as reference-tip keyframes with roll and opening.

**Verification.** I temporarily forced the scheduler to prefer drumming and traced the failures. That exposed and fixed four planning bugs: landing times slipping because the roll-up was re-anchored to the current tick; the lateral move being stretched over the available window; a dragged anchor being re-planned from the note's nominal lane rather than its actual position; and the roll-up fraction being reset by an already-landed chain head so the fingertip never cleared the contact band. With drumming forced, all 113 training notes complete with timing within about 10 ms, including taps during holds, same-lane repeats, drum landings onto slides, and chains after vanished notes. With normal costs the charts play exactly as before.

**Limits.** The minimum interval for re-using the same rolled fingertip is set at 0.2 s and has only been exercised at 0.25 s and above. A hold anchors the free fingertip to within 2.6 lanes, so taps far across the screen during a hold are still a hold-or-taps choice.

Revision 3 is in place. The final run completes 113/113 on the training charts, all hits perfect except one "great", with plan time well inside the 33 ms budget.

**What changed and why**

- **Fixed a latent crash in rocking landings.** Whenever the scheduler actually selected a rock landing, keyframe generation raised a KeyError on a missing field and the hand was lifted for that tick. The training charts never selected a rock under normal costs, so this never showed up in the score, but denser charts would have triggered it constantly. It surfaced when I ran the policy under synthetic load, and is now fixed.
- **Bounded the planning cost for dense charts.** I injected fake notes at 10 and 20 notes per second to measure the scheduler. At 20 notes per second the mean plan time was 20 ms with peaks of 44 ms, over budget. The planner now considers at most the 14 nearest upcoming notes per tick, limits rocking candidates to three per note, rejects impossible drum options early, and caches each state's lift-off pose. Under the same 20 notes per second load this brings plan time to about 1 ms mean, 9 ms peak.
- **Removed a bad pruning idea.** A first attempt also limited predecessors to events within 1 s, which wrongly prevented chaining an isolated tap into a chord 1.1 s later and cost a note. That window is gone; the note cap alone gives the speed-up.

**Verification.** Load tests at 10 and 20 notes per second run without errors. The normal evaluation is back to 113/113 with the same timing accuracy as before.

Revision 4 is in place. The final run again completes 113/113 on the training charts with timing unchanged (every hit perfect but one "great").

**What changed and why**

- **Exception safety net.** If planning ever throws on an unseen chart, the policy now keeps following its previous plan for that tick instead of lifting the hand in place, so a transient failure costs nothing and a mid-descent landing still completes.
- **Safer re-tap spacing.** The minimum interval between whole-hand re-touches moved from 0.19 s to 0.20 s, the value at which my earlier calibration showed no "not fresh" failures. Faster alternation still comes from rocking and drum landings.
- **Earlier hold release.** Contact on holds and slides is kept for 85% of the duration (plus a 20 ms margin) instead of 88%, since the judge needs 80%. This frees the hand sooner for the next note while measured contact still reads 100% on the training charts.
- **Diverging long-note chords.** When two held notes drift farther apart than the gripper can open, the hand now tracks the longer-lasting note exactly rather than splitting the error between both and risking both.
- **Late tolerance for plain landings** raised from 80 ms to 100 ms, since their timing scatter is only a few milliseconds. Rolled landings keep 80 ms.
